title: 9月の実質賃金 9カ月連続プラス
body: 物価の変動を反映した働く人1人あたりの今年9月の「実質賃金」が、前の年の同じ月と比べて2.2%増えました。10年ぶりとなる9か月連続のプラスです。【写真で見る】将来が不安で…若者が“NISA貧乏”に？若者の声は厚生労働省によりますと、基本給や残業代・ボーナスなどを合わせた働く人1人あたりの今年9月の現金給与の総額は31万1409円で、前の年の同じ月から4.6%増えました。およそ34年ぶりに、3%以上の伸び率が8か月続いています。また、物価の変動を反映した9月の「実質賃金」は、前の年の同じ月と比べて2.2%増えたということです。実質賃金は9か月連続でプラスとなっていて、2016年2月から2017年1月の12か月連続以来となる10年ぶりです。厚労省は実質賃金のプラスについて、「引き続き基本給などが上がっていることや、去年と比べて物価の上昇が落ち着いていることが要因だが、今後の動向を注視したい」としています。

title: サイバー攻撃で強制遮断検討 政府
body:
政府が近くまとめるサイバーセキュリティー緊急対策パッケージに、二次被害の防止対策として、ウェブサイトへの接続を強制的に遮断する「ブロッキング」の検討が盛り込まれることが分かった。「アクセス抑止策」として検討する。ＧＭＯインターネットの不正アクセス問題を巡って攻撃者が個人情報をサイトで公開する事例が発生している。漏えいした個人情報の悪用を防ぐため、ブロッキングをはじめとする対策の法的課題などを早急に検討する方針を示す。【一覧】サイバー攻撃で個人情報などの流出が判明した企業・団体と問い合わせ先
ブロッキングは、特定のサイトへの接続を強制的に遮断し、サイトを閲覧できなくする措置だ。ＧＭＯインターネットの不正アクセス問題を巡り、攻撃者が１０月２７日、不正に取得した個人情報をサイトで公開。総務省は「二次被害が拡大する現実的な恐れが生じている」などとして、同日付で国内の通信事業者に対し、サイトへのブロッキングを要請した。
今回の総務省の要請は妥当だったとする意見がある一方で、拙速だったとの批判も出ている。ブロッキングを実施するには、通信事業者が全利用者のすべての通信先を確認する必要がある。通信内容や宛先などを第三者に知られない権利は「通信の秘密」として憲法などで保障されており、これまでも実施に当たって慎重に検討が進められてきた経緯があるためだ。
一方、サイバー攻撃による相次ぐ個人情報の漏えいで、今後も攻撃者が個人情報を公開するといった行為に出る恐れがある。政府はブロッキングなどの対策を機動的に講じることができるよう、法的課題の検討を急ぐことにした。

title: 米加州 死刑囚548人を終身刑に
body: 【AFP＝時事】米カリフォルニア州のギャビン・ニューサム知事は5日、州内の死刑囚全員の刑を終身刑に減刑すると発表した。対象は500人を超える。【関連記事】米軍の銃殺刑生配信計画に非難殺到「米国はそこまで落ちぶれていない」2028年の大統領選への出馬が有力視されているニューサム氏は、死刑は全米で最も人口の多い同州の価値観と「相いれない」と述べた。「全カリフォルニア州民へ」と題した書簡で、「国家が認める殺害を拒むことで、私たちは個人としても集団としても、より強い社会を築けるという、長年抱いてきた揺るぎない信念に基づき、きょう行動する」と記した。同州では548人が死刑執行を待っており、死刑囚の数は世界でも有数となっている。裁判所は殺人などの重大犯罪で有罪となった被告に死刑を言い渡し続けているが、同州では20年間、死刑は執行されていない。ニューサム氏は5日の長文の書簡で、決定に至る思考の過程や、この問題をめぐって重ねてきたという議論を州民に説明した。死刑囚全員を一律に減刑するとの決定は、凶悪犯罪の被害者を区別しないという考えに基づくものだとした。「減刑の対象とする犯罪や犯罪者を選別しようとすれば、殺人被害者を、加害者が死刑に値するかどうかで意図せず二つに分けてしまうと結論付けた」と説明した。さらに、「従って、すべての死刑囚の刑を同じように、仮釈放の可能性のない終身刑に減刑する」と述べた。「これらの犯罪者は刑務所で死ぬことになる。しかし、それは私たちの手によるものではない」【翻訳編集】 AFPBB News

title: ルビオ長官 辞任検討の報道否定

title: 露 JT資産を同国企業の管理下に
body: ロシアのプーチン大統領は5日、日本たばこ産業（JT）がロシアに保有する資産を同国企業の一時管理下に移すよう命じた。【写真】日本たばこ産業（JT）社長大統領令に署名した。ロシアは最近、プーチン氏の北方領土訪問や北海道新聞記者の拘束など対日圧力を強めており、日本企業にも影響が及んだ形だ。一時管理制度は2023年、欧米などによるロシアの資産凍結に対抗するため大統領令に基づき設けられた。企業側は所有権を維持するが、事実上経営権を失う。インタファクス通信によれば、世界的なたばこ大手の資産がロシア企業の管理下に置かれるのは初という。JTの海外事業を手がける「JTインターナショナル」（JTI）のホームページによると、JTIは1999年からロシア事業を展開。07年にはロシアのたばこ市場で首位となった。ロシア国内には4カ所の生産拠点があり、従業員は約4000人に上る。JTは「従業員をはじめとするステークホルダーを最優先に、状況および今後取り得る選択肢について精査している」とコメントした。

title: 歴史的勝利 喜び広がるテキサス州
body: アメリカの中間選挙で、共和党の牙城とされるテキサス州の上院選を民主党候補が38年ぶりに制し、現地では歴史的な勝利に喜びが広がっています。3日に行われた上院選で勝利したのは、民主党のジェームズ・タラリコ氏（37）です。タラリコ氏は物価高対策や政治腐敗の一掃を訴え、トランプ大統領が支持する共和党候補を破りました。選挙から一夜明けた4日、現地で取材に応じた女性は「これほど希望を感じたのは本当に久しぶりです。夢がかなったような気持ちです」と喜びを語り、「少なくとも汚職を食い止めるチャンスが生まれました。今度はトランプ氏が弱い立場になったのです」と期待を寄せました。また、別の男性も「何度もこうなると聞かされながら、実現しませんでした。だから本当に実現したなんて、信じられない気持ちです」と驚きを語りました。歴史的な勝利を受け、テキサス州の中心都市オースティンでは、タラリコ氏のグッズが人気を集めています。地元の雑貨店では、タラリコ氏のグッズを求める支持者が相次いで訪れ、Tシャツ400枚と帽子200個が売り切れたほか、マグカップなどもほとんどが売り切れたということです。店長によりますと、これまで販売した政治家のグッズの中で、最も売れ行きがよいということです。

title: 米右派動揺「トランプ後」を模索
body:
【AFP＝時事】ドナルド・トランプ米大統領の支持層「MAGA（米国を再び偉大に）」派の熱狂はついに冷めたのか。米国の右派はトランプ氏のポピュリズム思想から脱却し、伝統的な保守主義に回帰するのだろうか。【写真】米中間選挙の共和党大敗、原因は対イラン戦争 バンス副大統領
トランプ氏に対する事実上の信任投票となった中間選挙で大敗を喫したことを受け、多くの共和党員が4日、党の将来と、その方向性を決める上でトランプ氏が今後どのような役割を果たすのか、あるいは役割が残されているのかについて疑問を抱いている。
伝統的な保守派の代表格である米紙ウォールストリート・ジャーナルの論説は、「自己反省」を求め、80代のトランプ氏を権力の座に押し上げた、極端な国家主義に基づくアイデンティティー重視の主張からの脱却を訴えた。
同紙の論説委員会は4日朝、「関税と大規模強制送還は、実質所得の増加に代わるものではない。MAGAの岩盤支持層である若い男性に迎合することは、3日に共和党を見限ったヒスパニック系や無党派層、郊外の浮動票層を取り込むことの代わりにはならない」と記した。
一方、ホワイトハウスにあまり反省の色は見られなかった。
4日のX（旧ツイッター）への最初の投稿には、険しい表情でにらみつけるトランプ氏の写真に「トランプ氏は今もなおあなたたちの大統領だ」という文字が重ねられていた。トランプ氏が2029年1月まで大統領職にとどまることができると念押しするものだった。
しかし、米国の政治日程は容赦なく進む。4日は事実上、トランプ氏の後任を選ぶ2028年大統領選に向けた選挙戦の幕開けとなった。
この争いにトランプ氏が加わることはもうない。3選は合衆国憲法で禁じられているからだ。
中間選挙の結果によってトランプ氏の政治的影響力が強まるというシナリオもあり得たが、現実はそうならなかった。
3日夜に共和党が喫した敗北は、民主党にとって最も楽観的なシナリオさえも超えるレベルの歴史的な大惨敗で、トランプ氏の影響力低下を加速させた。

title: バンス氏 米大統領と距離置く姿勢
body: （CNN）　米国のバンス副大統領は4日、中間選挙で共和党が惨敗した直接の原因はイラン戦争にあるとの認識を示した。【映像】イラン、地下トンネルに並ぶドローンの映像公開バンス氏はこの日午前、X（旧ツイッター）に長文を投稿し、「我々が負けた原因は戦争だ。大統領自身、昨夜そう言っていた」と述べた。バンス氏を巡っては、2028年大統領選への出馬を視野に入れているとの見方が多い。今回の投稿はトランプ大統領やその政策路線と距離を置く内容となった。バンス氏は「戦争にそれだけの価値があった、今後6年間にわたって上院の多数派を失うだけの価値があったと主張したいなら、そうすればいい。支払うに値する代償だったと主張すればいい。賛成するにせよ反対するにせよ、少なくともそのほうが誠実だ」とも述べた。そのうえで「だが、我々が負けた理由は誰もが分かっている。今後の方向性について少しでも率直に議論するなら、まずそこから始める必要がある」と言い添えた。バンス氏の見方では、トランプ氏の支持基盤の有権者は投票所には足を運んだものの、共和党に票を投じることはなかった。バンス氏は「もっと多くの有権者を投票に向かわせることができた地域もあっただろう。それは間違いない。だが、投票率は主要な問題ではない。主な問題は、24年にトランプ・バンス陣営に投票した多くの人が今回は民主党に票を入れたことだ」と指摘する。「何が起きたのか、なぜそうなったのかをめぐって今後、多くの内紛や議論が起きるはずだ。私が尊敬している世論調査の専門家の1人は、選挙戦の終盤、経済に関する我々の訴えが切れ味に欠けていたと話していた。それは事実だろう」「ただ、我々が負けた本当の理由は、ほぼ誰の目にも明らかだ」（バンス氏）トランプ氏もイランとの戦争の影響があったとの見方を示唆しているが、自身が始めた戦争を引き続き正当化している。トランプ氏は3日夜、FOXニュースとの電話インタビューで「イランも一因だったと思う。ただ同時に、国民はイランに対する私の措置の重要性を理解していた」と語った。

title: 経産省 中部電力に業務改善命令
body: 中部電力浜岡原発（静岡県御前崎市）の耐震設計データの不正など、中部電で不祥事が相次いだことを受け、経済産業省は6日、電気事業法に基づき中部電に業務の改善を命令した。データ不正のほか、社内のチェック体制や内部通報制度の機能不全などを問題視し、役員らの責任を明確化することなどを求めた。【図解】データねつ造…浜岡原発の不正はどう行われたのか浜岡原発を巡っては、3、4号機の再稼働に向けた原子力規制委員会の安全審査で、耐震設計の基準となる「基準地震動」を定める際に不正な操作をするなどしていた。このため、中部電は9月14日に外部の弁護士らによる調査委員会の報告書を公表。報告書は、不正の原因について、中部電に「独自の正当化理論」があったと指弾していた。このほか中部電では、廃炉作業が進む浜岡原発1、2号機で、廃炉費用を請求する書類で改ざんをしていたことが明らかになっている。さらに、中部電傘下の販売子会社「中部電力ミライズ」は、電気料金の一部メニューで本来より高い料金を徴収していた。こうした状況を踏まえ、経産省は中部電への処分を検討。社内に設けられた内部通報制度が機能せず、ガバナンス（企業統治）に不備があったと認定した。一連の不祥事には、背景に共通する課題があったとして、中部電の業務を抜本的に改善させる必要があると判断した。中部電への業務改善命令に関して、経産省から意見を求められていた電力・ガス取引監視等委員会も今月4日、命令に異存はないと回答した。命令では、原子力部門など専門性の高い部署の閉鎖的な組織風土を改め、社内のチェック機能を強化するよう要求。外部人材を活用して、再発防止策の実効性を検証する体制を整えることも求めた。経産省は今後、中部電に具体的な取り組みを盛り込んだ業務改善計画を提出させ、改善状況を継続的に確認する。【佐久間一輝】

title: NYダウ急落 一時1800ドル超安
body: 5日のニューヨーク株式市場でダウ工業株30種平均は急落し、下落幅は前日終値比で一時1800ドルを超えた。米中間選挙で野党・民主党が圧勝したことで人工知能（AI）の先行き懸念が一段と強まり、ハイテク株を中心に売りが拡大。前日の上昇分（1569ドル）を帳消しにする勢いとなっている。【一覧】日本は?　データセンターの稼働容量と成長率3日の中間選挙では、民主党が上下両院で過半数の議席を確保したほか、知事選でも民主党候補の躍進が目立った。電気代の高騰や水不足への懸念を背景に、高度なAI開発を支える大規模データセンター（DC）建設への規制強化を訴える候補者が多かった。同時に実施された住民投票でも、DC新設の一時停止を可決するケースが相次いだ。こうした結果を受け、投資家の間で半導体需要への悪影響やAI投資の停滞に対する懸念が膨らんだ。5日は主要な株価指数が軒並み大幅下落し、米半導体大手エヌビディアやブロードコムの株価が前日終値比8～9％程度の下落となっている。【ワシントン浅川大樹】

title: 9月の実質賃金 9カ月連続プラス
body: 物価の変動を反映した働く人1人あたりの今年9月の「実質賃金」が、前の年の同じ月と比べて2.2%増えました。10年ぶりとなる9か月連続のプラスです。【写真で見る】将来が不安で…若者が“NISA貧乏”に？若者の声は厚生労働省によりますと、基本給や残業代・ボーナスなどを合わせた働く人1人あたりの今年9月の現金給与の総額は31万1409円で、前の年の同じ月から4.6%増えました。およそ34年ぶりに、3%以上の伸び率が8か月続いています。また、物価の変動を反映した9月の「実質賃金」は、前の年の同じ月と比べて2.2%増えたということです。実質賃金は9か月連続でプラスとなっていて、2016年2月から2017年1月の12か月連続以来となる10年ぶりです。厚労省は実質賃金のプラスについて、「引き続き基本給などが上がっていることや、去年と比べて物価の上昇が落ち着いていることが要因だが、今後の動向を注視したい」としています。

title: 日本製紙 八代工場の紙生産断念へ
body: 日本製紙が、7月の熊本地震で被災した八代工場（熊本県八代市）について、紙・パルプの生産再開を断念する方針を固めたことが5日、分かった。【令和8年熊本地震】空から見た被害状況再建には巨額の費用が必要なことから、生産再開は難しいと判断したとみられる。拠点としては維持し、社員の雇用も継続する方向で、施設の活用策の検討を進める。日本製紙は6日に2026年9月中間決算の発表を予定しており、瀬辺明社長が出席し、八代工場の今後について説明する予定だ。

title: Major tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to fears of AI slowdown
summary: Markets have been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry following the US midterms.
body:
Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development.
Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025.
The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.
In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide.
The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%.
South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%.
The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling.
Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%.
It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen.
Democrats in races across the US campaigned to slow the growth of data centres and AI, and there were dozens of measures on ballots around the country aimed at restricting the development of the hubs crucial for powering the technology.
They won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of President Donald Trump's presidency.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.

In a social media post, Trump blamed the slide on his political opponents.
"The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election," he said.
"Remember, it wasn't Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN!"
Some Democrats have argued that AI has grown too big without any safeguards or oversight and have promised, with their new power in Congress, to change that.
"Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future. NATIONAL DATA CENTER MORATORIUM NOW," Democrat Senator Bernie Sanders said in a post on X on Thursday.
Shares in companies heavily exposed to AI data centres, including crucial chipmakers and semiconductor manufacturers, fell sharply on Thursday, highlighting investor concerns that had already been growing.
Nvidia shares slid more than 9%, knocking more than $400bn off the firm's market value.
Other chipmakers also suffered, with AMD and Micron both dropping by more than 17%. Intel shares also dropped, down 10.3%, while memory card maker SanDisk plunged more than 22%.
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which tracks the performance of 30 of the largest companies involved in semiconductor production, fell by more than 12%.
Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value on Thursday.
Musk hadspent nearly $450mbacking Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue inthe Democratic tsunamion Tuesday night.
In total, the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, have shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day.

title: Democratic socialist defeats incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayor's race
summary: The results mean America's two most populous cities - New York and Los Angeles - will be led by democratic socialists.
body:
Nithya Raman, once seen as a long-shot candidate, will be LA's new mayor
Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.
Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.
Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.
Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.
Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."
"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".
She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.
The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.
The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

Raman's win over Bass has all the appearances of echoing voter sentiment across the US as part of sweeping Democratic wins, including in deep-Republican country that hadn't seen liberal leaders in decades.
Washington DC also elected democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George as its new mayor, furthering progressive leadership in another major US city.
US President Donald Trump was asked at the White House about the wins by politicians on the left flank of the Democratic Party and said, "If you go by history, it's going to be a disaster".
Such candidates have become a focal point of attacks by Republicans.

title: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
body:
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

title: Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for second time in a week
summary: At least 21 flights across Europe are affected in what the UK government calls a "malicious hoax threat".
body:
The Aer Lingus plane at Evreux military air base in France after being diverted following a bomb threat
At least 21 aircraft and several airports across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats in the second such incident this week, with the UK calling it a "malicious hoax".
Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair's Helsinki-Rome flight.
EasyJet said itsflights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by police in Prague as a precaution. London Heathrow and Birmingham airports received threats that were assessed as not credible.
No explosives have been found during searches, and it is not clear if the incidents, some claimed by a little known group,are related.
Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email.
The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history".
They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.
These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports.
"Fighters of the Male State" likely refers to the Russian group "Muzhskoi Legion" ( "Male Legion") - an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet it retained tens of thousands of online followers as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But that email, even if genuine, is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
UK transport secretary says flights hit by 'hoax threats'
UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats."
She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats".
A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details.
Heathrow later said in a statement it had received a threat earlier in the day which was "deemed not credible", adding there was "no risk to passengers, colleagues or the aircraft".
"There are robust UK aviation security standards in place to assess and safely manage these types of situations," the statement said.
Meanwhile, a Birmingham Airport spokesperson told the BBC it had received a threat, after which "processes were immediately initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".
The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday:
Aer Lingus said its flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy, landing safely. The company added that it was working to "re-accommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible".
Two Finnair flights from Helsinki landed at their destinations as normal, the airline said. One was escorted into Rome's Fiumicino airport by Italian Air Force fighter jets, Aeroporti di Roma told the BBC, while the other landed in Vienna, Austria
Wizz Air said two flights which departed Milan were affected - one was heading to Warsaw, before being diverting to Vienna; the other landed safely in Bucharest, with teams inspecting the aircraft
Polish airline LOT said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed as planned, and "no suspicious items were found". Another LOT flight from Warsaw to Paris was stopped before take-off and the plane and baggage underwent a security screening, with no hazardous items found
Three Ryanair flights landed in Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian media - one from Copenhagen and another from Madrid landed in the capital Sofia, while a third coming from London bound for Sofia landed in Plovdiv. The flights were escorted by Bulgarian air force fighter jets
No explosives were found on four flights which landed in Prague, Czech police said. EasyJet later said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were among those affected. "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the company said
Aegean Airlines said it "was informed of a bomb threat" concerning two of its flights from Thessaloniki in Greece to Milan, and also from Athens to Vienna. It said threat was "unfounded", and both flights departed from the respective airports"
A Ryanair flight from Porto in Portugal landed safely in Milan as planned, with bomb disposal experts checking them on arrival, Italy's Ansa news agency reported
Spain's airport authority said it had received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport, but any threat was ruled out following inspections. Iberia later said two of its flights - Milan-Madrid and Rome-Madrid - were affected. It was not clear whether the third plane was the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight
Air Serbia said its flight from Belgrade to Bucharest "landed safely at its destination airport", and after checks, a reported bomb threat was "assessed as unfounded"
Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem.
Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify.
On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could."
Noble says she could hear fighter jets during the landing and saw one touch down behind the aircraft.
After landing at the Évreux-Fauville air base in Normandy, passengers learned the flight had been the subject of a bomb threat.
Emily Noble, a passenger on a diverted Aer Lingus flight, told the BBC she was now waiting for transfer to Rome at an air base in France
Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dogs.
The passengers were later told they would be taken to an airport in Paris and another plane would fly them on to Rome.
Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry, said the industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day" but he had been "surprised" by this week's incidents.
A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe there is a potential of explosive device on board", he said.
He said the concern was that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion".
Marco Chan, an aviation expert at Kingston University, told the BBC the threats were "most likely a hoax, but the system is right to treat it as real".
He said they were being viewed by some experts as "possibly part of a pattern of cheap, deniable disruption" to air travel.
Hoaxes can also come from copycats, he said, but "three days of incidents is too small a sample to separate coordination from contagion".
Two days ago, seven European flights, including two from the UK, were searched after bomb threats were made. No explosives were found on any of the planes after searches.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.

title: California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
summary: California has historically had the largest population of people on death row in the US.
body:
California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in January
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in Tennessee
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted thatFrançois Mitterrand did precisely thatin his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
San Quentin State Prison's used to house California's death row adjustment centre
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.
Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 whenthe governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.
Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.
"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.
"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
summary: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
body:
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.
The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with  legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".
It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog saidemployees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.
"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.
The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar tomeasures being introduced in the European Union.,external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

title: 'I was asked if I was a crier': Your worst job interviews revealed
summary: Bad job interviews can be horrible to experience in the moment, but there is a lot they can teach us about the world of work
body:
Watch: What was your worst ever job interview?
Tiara Allen arrived on time to interview for a retail job. Her interviewer didn't.
She waited for around 40 minutes in a shopping centre while the interviewer's co-worker called them "two or three times".
When they finally showed up, Tiara says she was told it was because the meeting wasn't in the schedule.
She needed work at the time, so took the job when she was offered it, but says she would handle the situation differently now.
"I would not take a job if they took that long," she says, adding that she believed her treatment during the interview was a sign of how the firm tended to treat staff.
Tiara Allen says she took the job despite being made to wait 40 minutes before the interview because she needed work
Tiara is far from alone. She is one of many people who spoke to the BBC about their worst job interview experiences after we wrote aboutthe one interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.
While those situations can be hard to deal with in the moment, they can also teach us a lot about the world of work.
During an interview for an assistant at a book publisher in New York, Chas Edwards was asked a question he wasn't expecting.
"I was asked for my first job if I was a crier," he recalls.
Thinking the interviewer was being funny, Chas replied that he didn't cry. He was later told that this was why he got the job.
"Her last assistant had cried – too often, I guess? – and she wanted someone who didn't cry. So she was being serious and I thought it was a joke," he says.
It was a bad sign. Chas says it was "a terrible, terrible job with a miserable boss" and while he managed to make it through 13 months there without crying he was "crying inside".
"I set the world record for working for this person. No-one had ever lasted three months with her before," he recalls.
Despite all this, Chas says he is in some ways grateful the experience was so awful.
"Because every job since then, even the bad ones, are not that bad," he says, adding that he can "cry anywhere now".
Chas Edwards says he thought the interviewer's question for his first job was a joke
Corinne Card also found herself floored when the first question she was asked in an interview for an administrative job was if she liked working with people.
When she replied yes, she was told that the job wouldn't be for her and the interview ended there.
"I don't know if it was a deliberate trap. Because who would answer 'I don't like working with people'?"
Corinne Mills, joint managing director of Personal Career Management, says that it can be worth asking an interviewer to clarify any weird questions, perhaps by repeating the question back to them.
However, if a line of questioning is really off-putting, she says it can also be a sign of what it's like to work there, saying that interviews are also about candidates judging the company.
Meanwhile, other questions are not just annoying – they are illegal.
Discrimination against a protected characteristic is against the law,external, meaning an employer cannot treat you less favourably based on your age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation.
Employment lawyer Roy Magara says that women being asked if they intend on having children in an interview is a "quite common" kind of bias. He says he has also seen a case where an older candidate was told he didn't get the job after an interview because he didn't fit the "vibe" of a younger team.
If you think these sorts of biases took place in your interview, Roy says you can send the companya subject access request,externalto see how they discussed your application internally.
Worst-case scenarios like these can make interviews feel very difficult, especially considering the control employers have over candidates.
Euan Cameron, co-founder of hiring software Willo, says that even with this power imbalance it's important not to overthink what an interview is.
"An interview is just a conversation between two people," he says.
Of course, as in Tiara's case, it helps when both of those people show up.

title: Interest rates hiked to 4% in first increase in over three years
summary: Most analysts expected the increase from 3.75% to 4%.
body:
Interest rates have risen for the first time in more than three years and the Bank of England has signalled a further increase is likely unless the US-Iran war is resolved.
Rates rose to 4% from 3.75% in a bid to curb inflation mainly driven by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.
Andrew Bailey, the Bank's governor, said the decision "shouldn't be seen as the first in an inevitable long sequence of hikes", but warned "unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, neither does it seem likely to be the last increase".
The higher level will increase the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, but will also lead to higher returns on savings.
The Bank's rate-setting committee all backed increasing interest rates, with eight out of nine voting in favour of the rise to 4%. One member wanted an even bigger increase to 4.25%.
Bailey said the hike was warranted due to higher energy prices and pointed to what happens in the Middle East as the main factor in future decisions.
"Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East," the governor said.
Bailey said he could "see the argument" for a further rate hike, before taking a "more conditional approach" dependent on the path of energy prices and inflation in the coming months.
However, the views of members on the rate-setting committee differed on the path forward.
Clare Lombardelli agreed there was "likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term", while Megan Greene went further, suggesting "additional hikes" might be likely depending on how inflation impacted wages, prices and the jobs market.
However, Alan Taylor said the rate rise was a "a risk-management 'one-for-now' insurance hike".
Inflation, which measures the pace of price rises over time, is well below its peak of a few years ago but remains above the Bank of England's 2% target and is expected to increase further next year.
Prices rose3.5% in the year to September 2026, largely due to higher fuel prices. Millions of households are also set to be hit by energy bill increases in January.
Higher fuel prices can lead to prices rising for a host of goods and staples as businesses pass on higher costs to customers.
But the Bank said there was "limited evidence" this had happened so far for goods, such as food, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower margins.
In an interview with the BBC, Bailey defended the decision to raise rates despite the Bank's assessment that inflation was yet to spread to other parts of the economy.
He said further increases in energy prices are putting upward pressure on inflation and "that's what we have to seek to lean against".
Patrick Bryson, from Brighton, is set to see his five-year mortgage term with a 3.51% interest rate end soon.
The best deal the 51-year-old can find is a 5.17% loan with HSBC, which means his repayments will jump from £1,420 to £1,680 a month from February.
"The only thing that bugs me about the mortgage is that after five years of paying it off we are now paying more than we were before," said the father-of-three. "That's a bit of a slap in the face."
The guitar teacher, who has a combined income of around £68,000 a year with his wife, who manages a care home, said the couple is feeling pressure on their finances and so have changed their shopping habits and are looking to reduce their subcription outgoings.
"Over the last year I have stopped buying wine, we don't go out to eat much anymore, we have knocked takeaways on the head. The prices are ridiculous," he said.
Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you

The Bank now expects inflation to peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year, higher than it originally estimated, and not return to 2% until 2028.
But in an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it suggested.
While the UK cannot control global energy prices, the Bank raised rates, for the first time since August 2023, in order to limit the knock-on effects of high energy prices resulting in inflation going up across the board.
Its base rate is what it charges other banks and building societies to borrow money, which influences what customers for mortgages, loans, credit cards get charged, as well as savings rates.
The rate rise will see 510,000 tracker mortgage-holders see a £31 monthly jump in repayments, according to banking trade body UK Finance.
Homeowners on fixed deals will see no change, though future products may be affected.
However, people on variable deals will be impacted depending on how their lender reacts to the rate rise. Typically a 0.25pp rise means a £14 increase per month in repayments.

title: Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?
summary: The BBC's economics editor views one more interest rate as likely, but thinks that will be all.
body:
Interest rates have risen to 4% and the Bank of England has indicated there are more rises to come. The question is how many? There is a split on the rate-setting committee here.
Three of the nine voting members referred to "rises" plural. One member voted for a bigger increase, to 4.25%. Three referred to just one more including governor Andrew Bailey.
My read on this is that the expectation is for one more rise in February. Two and done, but it depends.
It is painful for those on variable mortgages, but should not be seen as the start of a cycle of hikes.
Predicting where interest rates will go is like throwing darts at a board that constantly moves around the wall, with expectations of how long the Iran War will last and its impact on the economy and prices lurching from day to day.
At least there is no blindfold.
The Bank's forecasts indicate inflation is heading to just under 5% next spring as a typical household energy bill surges by 27% in January to £2,150 a year.
Why have they raised now? High and rising inflation risks a further cycle of self fulfilling expectations of rising prices. It hasn't been seen so far, however. The war has lasted for 9 months, and led to oil prices used in the forecast averaging $108 a barrel.
And yet on the day they have announced the rate rise, the oil price is actually 13% lower than that having fallen in the run up and after the US mid term elections, reflecting expectations or guesses that President Trump will now retreat or deescalate from the Iran war.
The other notable factor is that the UK economy is performing much better than forecasts and expectations. This is underlined by the Bank of England's latest forecasts.
Growth has been 0.6%, and 0.5% in the first two quarters of the year. It is heading for 0.7%, the Bank said, between July and September, before slowing in the three months to the end of the year. Unemployment has stabilised, actually falling a little.
Some of this has fed throughinto a better performing currency, with sterling at its highest level since the Brexit referendum, when measured against a basket of currencies. This can help rein in inflation by making imports cheaper.
So, this is an unusual type of uncertainty. Even the expected further rise, probably in February next year is conditional on the war continuing.
The Bank of England stopped waiting for President Trump's war to end today, but perhaps the Democrats' resounding victory in the US midterm elections will stop the inflationary wave? The Bank has thrown a tentative first dart, and there is probably another to come.

title: More Mandelson papers set to be published before Christmas
summary: Documents were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a police investigation.
body:
The government is preparing to publish more documents about the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador.
Batches of papers were published in March and June - but others were withheld because they were part of a Metropolitan Police investigation.
The Cabinet Office has now said a number of extra documents will be published, likely before Christmas. Some will still be withheld at the request of the Met.
Cat Little, permanent secretary at the Cabinet Office, said that some of the documents could "now be published without prejudicing their investigation".
The Met Police had launched an investigation over allegations that, while he was serving as a government minister, Lord Mandelson had passed on market-sensitive government information to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Writing to the chair of Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee, Little said: "The Cabinet Office is now beginning the process to prepare these documents so that they may be laid before the House in response to the humble address motion as soon as possible."
She said the documents would be reviewed and in some instances may need to be redacted "for the purposes of avoiding prejudice to national security or international relations".
The process is expected to be completed before Parliament rises for the Christmas recess on 17 December.
Lord Mandelson was arrested on 23 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office.
He has repeatedly let it be known that he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.
"Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing," the Met Police said in a statement.
The lifelong Labour politician became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025, but was sacked in September after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with Epstein had emerged.
After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.
Mike Wood, shadow Cabinet Office minister, said: "We still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal.
"Labour did their utmost to hold this information back and it was only released because of the Conservatives humble address."

title: Putin not invited to G20 summit in Manchester, says Burnham
summary: The prime minister has said sanctions against Russia mean Putin will not attend the summit in November 2027.
body:
Putin, seen here during a speech in Moscow on Wednesday, has been missing from G20 summits since the Ukraine war
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Vladimir Putin is not invited to the G20 summit in Manchester.
Asked whether the Russian president would be invited to the annual meeting, which the UK is hosting in November 2027, Burnham said "no" because of sanctions against the Kremlin.
The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
But US president Donald Trump has sparked controversy by inviting Putin to this year's G20, which he will host in Miami in December. The Kremlin has not yet said whether Putin will attend.
Russia is amember of the G20- a group of 19 nations, the European Union and African Union - while Ukraine is not, but the ongoing war in Ukraine has loomed large over recent summits.
Putin has not attended any major global summit since he launched his invasion and ongoing war in Ukraine.
Asked about inviting him to the G20 in Manchester in 2027, Burnham told The Economist he "will not be coming because of an outstanding sanction" on senior Russian figures.
He said the meeting would provide "a real opportunity" to work with Chinese president Xi Jinping on safety regulations for artificial intelligence (AI).
Pressed on whether the UK could bring the US and China around the same table to agree on global AI supervision, Burnham said: "As I sit here today, that feels challenging, but we've got to hold out the need to find global agreements on AI.
"If we don't, the risks of recent times will magnify, they will significantly intensify.
"So you've got to go into it with that aim."
His decision not to include Putin in next year's gathering in Manchester comes after European diplomatsrefused to stand for an official photowith Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in October.
The so-called "family photo" would usually include representatives from all nations in attendance, but this year it was cancelled.
The US decision to invite Lavrov in the first place - which itself came afterfurther public rowsbetween Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky - also attracted criticism.
Discussing Ukraine, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told Lavrov at the summit: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is."
The UK last hosted the G20 summit in 2009.Next year's two-day eventwill take place in the Manchester Central Convention Centre in Manchester city centre and host thousands of diplomats and delegates, as well as world leaders.
The government has said it will use its G20 presidency in 2027 to "reinforce global economic stability" and "benefit people in every part of the UK".

title: Farage says he is worried Trump will step up Iran war after midterm 'disaster'
summary: Donald Trump "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war, Reform UK leader adds.
body:
Nigel Farage has long been a friend of Donald Trump
Nigel Farage has said he fears Donald Trump will "aggressively" continue his war with Iran after his "disaster" in the US midterm elections.
The Reform UK leader said the US president was still a friend, but accused him of having "broke a promise" to the American electorate by launching the war.
The war in Iran, which the US began in February 2026, weighed heavily in the midterm election results earlier this week in which theDemocrats swept Trump's Republicans out of powerin Congress.
Farage, who had initially urged people to support the war, said that following the election results he worried Trump would respond with more strikes on Iran.
Asked how he thinks President Trump will respond, Farage told broadcasters on Thursday: "I suppose I worry that the president will continue aggressively attacking Iran.
"That worries me because that would have even more serious implications for the price of oil, for inflation, for the whole western world".
He acknowledged he had initially supported the war but stressed he "never supported endless war".
Asked if the war was a mistake, he said: "There's no question about it."
The US president had "always kept his promises," added Farage, but "in this case, he said no more foreign wars and here we are in month eight of a war with no sign of ending."
"That and the resulting fuel prices are what in the end has done the damage."
Trump said on Tuesday that the poor results for Republican congressional candidates were partly due to the war and the related surge in oil prices.
But he insisted he did not regret launching a joint attack with Israel on Iran.
With Congress flipped, what does Trump do next?
In recent weeks, Trump has warned the US and Israel could return to all-out war after the midterms if a deal to end the conflict cannot be reached with Iran.
There have been various warnings, including from politicians in the UK, that Trump may now step up his attacks on Iran but Farage's criticism was more vocal than many have been.
Prime Minister Andy Burnhamsaid earlier this weekhe hoped the midterm results meant there was an "opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".
Farage said he had not spoken to Trump since the midterms but described it as a "complete wipeout" and "an absolute shellacking" for the Republicans.

"Trump has had an amazing career - he has beaten the pollsters, he has gone way beyond expectations," he added.
"This was his last big election and they all say, that all political careers end in failure."
His comments came at an event to announce Reform's first defence spokesperson, after the party was criticised for not having one.
Angus MacIntyre said he had stood down from a 40-year military career, including as a Wing Commander in the Royal Air Force (RAF), to take on the role.
MacIntyre pledged in a speech to end prosecutions of serving military personnel and veterans within the first 100 days of a Reform government.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch had criticised Reform for lacking a defence spokesperson despite having dedicated posts for immigration, the economy and education.
Farage said MacIntyre would form part of "a team we will build to represent us" on the issues of defence, security and cybersecurity.
